name: Juvelook

lead: Juvelook is a poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) injectable from VAIM Inc. of Seoul, used by clinicians as a skin booster and collagen stimulator under the eyes, in nasolabial folds, forehead, cheeks, clavicle and pores. People use it for smoother tear troughs, softer folds and better skin texture.

PDLLA is described as a biostimulator that prompts the body to produce collagen over time, so skin thickens and firms. Published reports describe a PDLLA and hyaluronic acid hybrid, with variants named Juvelook Volume and Juvelook GLAM. The literature is mainly small studies, case series and case reports, plus animal research.

paras: A clinician injects it, usually in a short series of sessions, with improvement building gradually as collagen forms.
Reported problems include firm nodules after tear trough injection, and a rabbit study examined accidental intra-arterial injection. It is performed by trained clinicians.

angle.text: People use Juvelook to smooth tear troughs and folds and improve skin texture. The PDLLA stimulates collagen so skin thickens and firms over time. Support comes from small studies and case reports.

lead: Juvelook is an injectable poly-D,L-lactic acid (PDLLA) product made by VAIM Inc. of Seoul, South Korea, used in aesthetic medicine as a skin booster and collagen-stimulating agent. Published reports describe a PDLLA and hyaluronic acid (HA) hybrid formulation, with variants named Juvelook, Juvelook Volume and Juvelook GLAM.[1][2][3][4]

People have it injected to improve under-eye hollows, nasolabial folds, sunken lateral cheeks, forehead contour, skin texture and pores, and body areas such as the clavicle and hips. The chain is: injected microspheres and HA carrier give some immediate volume, and the PDLLA is then described as stimulating the body's own collagen over weeks, thickening and smoothing the treated area.[1][5][1]

The literature consists mainly of case reports, case series and small clinical studies, many from Korean clinics, plus animal research and reports of complications such as nodules and, in a 2026 expert consensus, rare vascular events including visual impairment from inadvertent intravascular injection.[6][1][7][8][9][3][10][4]
infobox: Poly-D,L-lactic acid microspheres with non-cross-linked hyaluronic acid
Tear trough, nasolabial folds, forehead, cheeks, skin texture, clavicle, hips
Physician or trained injector (needle or cannula)

paras: Juvelook belongs to the class of collagen biostimulators, which differ from classic hyaluronic acid fillers because they are designed to provoke gradual tissue change rather than only occupy space. A 2026 consensus paper describes PDLLA-HA as a next-generation injectable that combines the collagen-stimulating property of PDLLA microspheres with non-cross-linked HA as a carrier.[4] A 2025 case report notes that the HA/PDLLA hybrid shows immediate volumisation through gain in skin thickness and a secondary delayed collagen effect.[5]

Wikipedia's polylactic acid article notes that the related poly-L-lactic acid is the active ingredient of Sculptra, an injectable facial volumiser, and that PLLA is described as prompting macrophages to release signalling molecules such as TGF-beta that lead fibroblasts to make collagen.[11] The D,L form in Juvelook is a different stereoisomeric mix of the polymer.

Reports describe both a more diluted skin-booster use, with small intradermal or topical-with-microneedling applications for texture and pores, and a higher-volume volumising use under the skin or in deeper planes, including with cannulas.[7][12][3][10]

Studies have examined Juvelook for lower eyelid or tear trough rejuvenation in Korean women,[1] nasolabial fold correction,[10] lateral sunken cheek (subzygomatic depression),[9] clavicular augmentation using a cannula,[3] forehead augmentation combined with autologous fat transfer,[8] and, in a case series, facial pore reduction with microneedling and topical application.[7]

A 2026 case series reported non-surgical hip augmentation with the GLAM variant in 30 Korean women, noting growing demand for non-surgical body contouring particularly in Asian populations.[13] A 2026 report also described combining PDLLA with gas subcision for atrophic acne scars.[14]

A 2026 study described a hybrid biostimulator and HA approach for tear trough rejuvenation.[15] The forehead paper frames a smooth, convex forehead as aesthetically desirable in Asian populations and lists limitations of implants, HA fillers and fat alone that the sequential approach aims to address.[8] The lateral sunken cheek paper notes that taut retaining ligaments can make smooth correction with conventional HA filler difficult and describes a cannula-based, highly diluted technique.[9]

Juvelook is part of the wave of Korean skin-booster and biostimulator products used in aesthetic clinics, where treatment is typically performed in repeated sessions weeks apart; the pain study, for example, treated cheeks over four sessions at three-week intervals.[12] Clinics and manufacturers market products by variant name, and the product appears under other names in some markets, since the 2026 consensus refers to PDLLA-HA 200 as Juvelook Volume/Lenisna.[4] Product-specific information on regulatory approvals differs by country and is not described in the published studies cited here.

A 2025 study evaluated PDLLA (Juvelook) for tear trough deformities in Korean women, with assessment before treatment and at one week, one month and six months using the Hirmand classification and satisfaction scores; the authors reported significant improvement, high satisfaction, minimal adverse effects and no severe complications.[1] A case report used ultrasound and radiological patterns to document collagen stimulation and tear trough enhancement,[5] and a separate 2026 paper examined a hybrid biostimulator with HA for tear troughs.[15]

A case series of microneedling combined with topical Juvelook assessed pore size and skin texture.[7] A study of forehead augmentation evaluated 12-month safety, efficacy and volume stability of sequential PDLLA and fat transfer.[8] Further reports address subzygomatic depression, nasolabial folds, clavicular augmentation and hip augmentation.[9][10][3][13]

A study of 20 Korean patients aged 22 to 67 who received intradermal PDLLA skin-booster injections in both cheeks over four sessions found higher pain scores on the left side, with male-female differences fading over repeated sessions.[12] Most of these reports are small, uncontrolled or case-level.

A case report described a 42-year-old woman who developed firm, non-inflammatory nodules about three weeks after PDLLA injection in the tear trough; a monopolar radiofrequency device was used and the authors reported complete resolution of the nodules within 24 hours.[6]

A 2026 consensus statement from oculoplastic surgeons, dermatologists and aesthetic physicians addresses safe injection technique and a management algorithm for PDLLA-HA-induced visual impairment, which it calls a rare but devastating complication of inadvertent intravascular injection.[4] A 2026 rabbit ear study investigated vascular behaviour and tissue response after intra-arterial injection of Juvelook and Juvelook Volume.[2] Animal findings do not establish human risk rates.
